newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila industry checks TCK wheat purchase report.
newsitem.headline: Manila industry checks TCK wheat purchase report.

text.p: Philippine flour executives said on Thursday they were checking reports that three local firms had bought 35,000 tonnes of fungus-infested U.S. wheat rejected by China but doubted they were true.
"I do not believe there were any purchases done, although some of our members have received offers," said Ric Pinca, executive director of the Philippine Association of Flour Millers Inc (PAFMIL).
Pinca, however, said he had asked PAFMIL members if they had bought any wheat rejected by China.
PAFMIL, whose members account for 80 percent of Philippine wheat imports, said local millers usually only buy dark northern spring wheat and western white wheat.
Traders said on Wednesday that three Philippine millers had bought 35,000 tonnes of U.S. soft winter wheat, reportedly containing the TCK smut fungus and rejected by China.
They said the wheat was bought at a discounted price of $192 a tonne as against a prevailing world market price of around $230 a tonne.
The deal was part of around 150,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat turned back by China and left sitting in two ships off Shanghaii and Fuzhou, the traders, who declined to be identified said.
But local flour executives said they doubted that the wheat, was fungus-tainted.
"They (American traders) have certification that the wheat was clean when it left U.S. ports," said one local flour executive who declined to be named.
Philippine quarantine officials said they have not received any information on fungus-tainted U.S. wheat shipments on their way to local ports.
"All commodity shipments in Philippine ports are checked by our employees for any infestation," said an official of the plant quarantine office of the Bureau of Plant Industry.
In Taiwan, traders said the island's regular wheat buying group always bought U.S. No.1 wheat and would not consider the lower grade wheat parked at Chinese ports.
South Korean buyers said wheat containing TCK was not permitted to enter the country for human consumption, but could be used for feed grain.
